Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 9.pdf ---
Core Financial System (FFMIA Compliance Initiative)
So here's where we are. We've got this thing hanging over us with FFMIA — basically the
law says our financial management system has to substantially comply with a whole set of
federal requirements, and right now nobody's totally confident we'd pass if someone came
in and checked us against that standard tomorrow. So the real driver here isn't "let's build
something cool," it's "we need a system that can actually stand up when auditors or the
inspector general come knocking and ask us to prove our books are clean and under
control."
The core of it is the general ledger — that's really the heart of everything, every other piece
hangs off of it. We need to be able to classify and track transactions properly: by fund, by
program, by organization, by project, by cost center, all that breakdown, because that's
how budget and program managers actually slice and dice the data later. On top of that we
need solid control over funds so we never end up obligating or spending more than what
was actually appropriated to us, that's a hard line, not negotiable. Then there's the
payment side — vendors, payees, getting money out the door correctly and being able to
track and confirm that a payment actually went where it should. And on the flip side, we
need to handle money coming in too, recording what's owed to the agency and following
up when people don't pay.
Cost management is something we want in there as well, even if it's not glamorous —
being able to actually measure what programs cost and what they're producing matters a
lot for budget conversations down the line. And reporting ties the whole thing together:
management needs timely numbers to make decisions, and we have to be able to produce
the formal financial statements and reports that get sent up the chain, to oversight bodies
and eventually made public.
Who's going to be touching this thing day to day: financial systems analysts, accountants,
program managers, the people who actually run agency operations and need to pull
numbers, and then auditors who'll come in periodically and poke at everything. So usability
for non-technical finance folks matters, this can't be something only an IT person can
operate.
On the technical side we do care about things like making sure it can handle the workload
without falling over, that it talks properly with other systems we already have instead of
becoming an island, that there's a real audit trail and security around who can touch what,
and decent web access so people aren't stuck only using it from one terminal somewhere.
That said, some of the fancier stuff — bells and whistles that are "nice to have" rather than
something a law or regulation forces on us — that's not where we want to spend our first
round of effort. If it's not mandatory and it's not clearly going to make somebody's job
dramatically easier, it can wait, we shouldn't be chasing every optional feature in the first
pass. The priority is getting the mandatory groundwork solid first.

Sistema: Core Financial System

Resumo executivo: The Core Financial System is a financial management solution intended to substantially comply with FFMIA requirements and provide auditable control over agency financial operations. It centralizes general ledger, fund control, payments, receivables, cost management, and financial reporting, enabling accurate accountability, prevention of unauthorized expenditures, operational decision-making, and evidence-based audits.

Escopo: The system shall record, control, process, audit, and report the agency's core financial transactions.
  Em escopo: General ledger and multidimensional transaction classification
  Em escopo: Fund appropriation, obligation, expenditure, and availability control
  Em escopo: Vendor and payee payment processing and tracking
  Em escopo: Accounts receivable and collection follow-up
  Em escopo: Program cost and output measurement
  Em escopo: Management and formal financial reporting
  Em escopo: Audit trail and access control
  Em escopo: Web-based access
  Em escopo: Integration with existing agency systems
  Fora de escopo: Optional bells-and-whistles not required for compliance or substantial job improvement — deferred from the first release
  Fora de escopo: Automated public publication of reports — the first release shall produce reports for subsequent publication
  Fora de escopo: Replacement of all existing agency systems — only required financial integrations are included

  Restrição: REST-03 (Control): The system shall prevent obligations or expenditures exceeding available appropriations.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Technology): The system shall be accessible through a web interface.
  Restrição: REST-05 (Integration): The system shall interoperate with existing agency systems where financial data exchange is required.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Financial Systems Analyst (Usuário primário): Configure financial structures, monitor integrations, investigate processing issues, and support system operation.
  STK-02 - Accountant (Usuário primário): Record and reconcile financial transactions, manage ledger data, process payments and receivables, and produce financial reports.
  STK-03 - Program Manager (Usuário primário): Monitor program funds, costs, outputs, obligations, expenditures, and management reports.
  STK-04 - Agency Operations Manager (Usuário secundário): Access operational financial information and use timely reports for decision-making.
  STK-05 - Auditor or Inspector General (Stakeholder externo): Examine financial records, control evidence, user actions, transactions, and reports.
  STK-06 - Oversight Body (Stakeholder externo): Receive formal financial statements and reports required for oversight.
  STK-07 - General Public (Stakeholder externo): Access financial reports designated for public disclosure through external publication processes.
  STK-08 - Existing Agency Systems (Stakeholder externo): Exchange required financial data with the Core Financial System through defined interfaces.

Regras de negócio:

  RN-004 - Financial accountability: Financial records must be complete, traceable, and available as evidence of financial control.
  RN-005 - Payment destination: A payment must be associated with an authorized vendor or payee and its destination must be confirmable.
  RN-006 - Receivable follow-up: Amounts owed to the agency must be recorded and monitored until collection, adjustment, or authorized closure.

  UC-001 - Record and classify ledger transaction | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant selects the ledger transaction function.
    2. The system displays the transaction-entry form.
    3. The accountant enters the transaction and applicable dimensions.
    4. The system validates the required data.
    5. The system records the transaction and audit event.
  UC-002 - Query classified transactions | Ator: Program Manager
    1. The user selects one or more financial dimensions.
    2. The system validates the user's access scope.
    3. The system retrieves matching transactions.
    4. The system displays the results.
  UC-003 - Control available appropriations | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant registers or selects an appropriation.
    2. The accountant submits an obligation.
    3. The system calculates available appropriation.
    4. The system records the obligation when the balance is sufficient.
  UC-004 - Process and confirm payment | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant selects a vendor or payee.
    2. The accountant enters payment details.
    3. The system validates the destination.
    4. The system records the payment.
    5. The system records payment confirmation.
  UC-005 - Manage receivable | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant creates a receivable.
    2. The accountant enters the amount, debtor, due date, and reference.
    3. The system validates the data.
    4. The system records the receivable with status 'Open'.
    5. The accountant records follow-up actions when applicable.
  UC-006 - Measure program cost and output | Ator: Program Manager
    1. The program manager selects a program and period.
    2. The system calculates recorded program costs.
    3. The program manager enters or reviews output measures.
    4. The system displays the cost and output result.
  UC-007 - Generate management report | Ator: Agency Operations Manager
    1. The manager selects a reporting period and classification.
    2. The system validates the selection.
    3. The system consolidates the financial data.
    4. The system generates the management report.
  UC-008 - Generate and export formal statement | Ator: Accountant
    1. The accountant selects the reporting period.
    2. The system validates the period.
    3. The system generates the formal statement.
    4. The accountant selects the oversight export option.
    5. The system creates the export file.
  UC-009 - Review audit evidence | Ator: Auditor or Inspector General
    1. The auditor selects an audit period, user, action, or record.
    2. The system applies the auditor's access scope.
    3. The system retrieves matching audit events.
    4. The system displays event details and linked records.
  UC-010 - Exchange data with existing agency system | Ator: Financial Systems Analyst
    1. The analyst initiates or schedules a data exchange.
    2. The system validates the data structure.
    3. The system transmits or receives the data.
    4. The system records the integration outcome.

Glossário:
  FFMIA: Federal Financial Management Improvement Act, the federal compliance driver identified for the financial management initiative.
  General ledger: The central accounting record containing the agency's financial transactions and balances.
  Appropriation: Authorized funding made available for agency obligations and expenditures.
  Obligation: A commitment of appropriated funds for a financial purpose.
  Expenditure: A disbursement or use of funds associated with an authorized financial activity.
  Fund: A financial classification used to identify a source or purpose of available resources.
  Program: An agency activity or initiative to which financial transactions and outputs are associated.
  Cost center: An organizational or operational classification used to assign and analyze costs.
  Receivable: An amount owed to the agency and subject to collection, adjustment, or authorized closure.
  Audit trail: A chronological record of user actions and system events affecting financial data.
  Oversight body: An external authority that receives or reviews formal agency financial information.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.

Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK

negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.

A ISO/IEC 25010:2023 define 9 características de qualidade do produto. Todo RNF deve ser 
classificado em uma dessas características. A seguir, cada característica com seus sub-atributos e 
exemplo de RNF.
1. Functional Suitability (Adequação Funcional)
 Functional Completeness — o sistema oferece todas as funções necessárias.
 Functional Correctness — as funções produzem os resultados corretos.
 Functional Appropriateness — as funções facilitam a realização das tarefas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 1. Functional Suitability
O sistema deve calcular o imposto sobre o valor do pedido aplicando corretamente a alíquota de ICMS 
vigente para o estado de destino, conforme tabela oficial CONFAZ, com variação máxima de R$ 0,01 em 
relação ao valor de referência da Receita Estadual.
2. Performance Efficiency (Eficiência de Desempenho)
 Time Behaviour — tempo de resposta e throughput.
 Resource Utilisation — uso de CPU, memória, rede.
 Capacity — limites máximos suportados.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 2. Performance Efficiency
O sistema deve processar no mínimo 200 pedidos por minuto sob carga de 1.000 usuários simultâneos, com 
tempo de resposta inferior a 2 segundos no percentil 95.
3. Compatibility (Compatibilidade)
 Co-existence — coexiste com outros sistemas sem degradação.
 Interoperability — troca dados com outros sistemas.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 3. Compatibility
A API do sistema deve expor endpoints REST/JSON compatíveis com o padrão OpenAPI 3.0, permitindo 
integração com o ERP legado via OAuth 2.0 sem modificações no ERP.4. Interaction Capability (Capacidade de Interação) — antes 'Usabilidade'
 Appropriateness Recognisability — usuário reconhece a adequação do sistema.
 Learnability — facilidade de aprendizado.
 Operability — facilidade de operação.
 User Error Protection — proteção contra erros do usuário.
 User Engagement — interface envolvente e motivadora.
 Inclusivity — acessível a pessoas com diferentes capacidades.
 User Assistance — suporte ao usuário.
 Self-Descriptiveness — interface autoexplicativa.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 4. Interaction Capability
Um usuário sem treinamento prévio deve ser capaz de registrar seu primeiro pedido completo em até 10 
minutos. A interface deve seguir as diretrizes WCAG 2.1 nível AA.
5. Reliability (Confiabilidade)
 Faultlessness — ausência de falhas em condições normais.
 Availability — proporção de tempo em que o sistema está operacional.
 Fault Tolerance — operação correta mesmo com falhas parciais.
 Recoverability — recuperação após falha.
EXEMPLO — RNF — 5. Reliability
O sistema deve ter disponibilidade mínima de 99,5% ao mês (máx. 3,6h de downtime não planejado). Em

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

Core Financial System (FFMIA Compliance Initiative)
So here's where we are. We've got this thing hanging over us with FFMIA — basically the
law says our financial management system has to substantially comply with a whole set of
federal requirements, and right now nobody's totally confident we'd pass if someone came
in and checked us against that standard tomorrow. So the real driver here isn't "let's build
something cool," it's "we need a system that can actually stand up when auditors or the
inspector general come knocking and ask us to prove our books are clean and under
control."
The core of it is the general ledger — that's really the heart of everything, every other piece
hangs off of it. We need to be able to classify and track transactions properly: by fund, by
program, by organization, by project, by cost center, all that breakdown, because that's
how budget and program managers actually slice and dice the data later. On top of that we
need solid control over funds so we never end up obligating or spending more than what
was actually appropriated to us, that's a hard line, not negotiable. Then there's the
payment side — vendors, payees, getting money out the door correctly and being able to
track and confirm that a payment actually went where it should. And on the flip side, we
need to handle money coming in too, recording what's owed to the agency and following
up when people don't pay.
Cost management is something we want in there as well, even if it's not glamorous —
being able to actually measure what programs cost and what they're producing matters a
lot for budget conversations down the line. And reporting ties the whole thing together:
management needs timely numbers to make decisions, and we have to be able to produce
the formal financial statements and reports that get sent up the chain, to oversight bodies
and eventually made public.
Who's going to be touching this thing day to day: financial systems analysts, accountants,
program managers, the people who actually run agency operations and need to pull
numbers, and then auditors who'll come in periodically and poke at everything. So usability
for non-technical finance folks matters, this can't be something only an IT person can
operate.
On the technical side we do care about things like making sure it can handle the workload
without falling over, that it talks properly with other systems we already have instead of
becoming an island, that there's a real audit trail and security around who can touch what,
and decent web access so people aren't stuck only using it from one terminal somewhere.
That said, some of the fancier stuff — bells and whistles that are "nice to have" rather than
something a law or regulation forces on us — that's not where we want to spend our first
round of effort. If it's not mandatory and it's not clearly going to make somebody's job
dramatically easier, it can wait, we shouldn't be chasing every optional feature in the first
pass. The priority is getting the mandatory groundwork solid first.

If developers build exactly what 
customers initially request, they’ll probably have to build it again because customers often don’t 
know what they really need. In addition, the BAs might not be talking to the right people or asking 
the right questions.
The features that users present as their “wants” don’t necessarily equate to the functionality they 
need to perform their tasks with the new product. To gain a more accurate view of user needs, the 
business analyst must collect a wide range of user input, analyze and clarify it, and specify just what 
needs to be built to let users do their jobs. The BA has the lead responsibility for recording the new 
system’s necessary capabilities and properties and for communicating that information to other 
stakeholders. This is an iterative process that takes time. If you don’t invest the time to achieve this 
shared understanding—this common vision of the intended product—the certain outcomes are 
rework, missed deadlines, cost overruns, and customer dissatisfaction.
User classes
People often talk about “the user” for a software system as though all users belong to a monolithic 
group with similar characteristics and needs. In reality, most products of any size appeal to a diversity 
of users with different expectations and goals. Rather than thinking of “the user” in singular, spend 
some time identifying the multiple user classes and their roles and privileges for your product.
Classifying users
Chapter 2 described many of the types of stakeholders that a project might have. As shown in 
Figure 6-1, a user class is a subset of the product’s users, which is a subset of the product’s customers, 
which is a subset of its stakeholders. An individual can belong to multiple user classes. For example, 
an application’s administrator might also interact with it as an ordinary user at times. A product’s 
users might differ—among other ways—in the following respects, and you can group users into a 
number of distinct user classes based on these sorts of differences:
■ Their access privilege or security levels (such as ordinary user, guest user, administrator)
■ The tasks they perform during their business operations
■ The features they use
■ The frequency with which they use the product
■ Their application domain experience and computer systems expertise
■ The platforms they will be using (desktop PCs, laptop PCs, tablets, smartphones, specialized 
devices)CHAPTER 6 Finding the voice of the user 103
■ Their native language
■ Whether they will interact with the system directly or indirectly
FIGURE 6-1 A hierarchy of stakeholders, customers, users, and user classes.
It’s tempting to group users into classes based on their geographical location or the kind of 
company they work in. One company that creates software used in the banking industry initially 
considered distinguishing users based on whether they worked in a large commercial bank, a small 
commercial bank, a savings and loan institution, or a credit union. These distinctions really represent 
different market segments, though, not different user classes.
A better way to identify user classes is to think about the tasks that various users will perform with 
the system. All of those types of financial institutions will have tellers, employees who process loan 
applications, business bankers, and so forth. The individuals who perform such activities—whether 
they are job titles or simply roles—will have similar functional needs for the system across all of the 
financial institutions. Tellers all have to do more or less the same things, business bankers do more or 
less the same things, and so on. More logical user class names for a banking system therefore might 
include teller, loan officer, business banker, and branch manager. You might discover additional user 
classes by thinking of possible use cases, user stories, and process flows and who might perform them.

396 PART III Requirements for specific project classes
Prioritizing by using business objectives
Enhancement projects are undertaken to add new capabilities to an existing application. It’s easy 
to get caught up in the excitement and start adding unnecessary capabilities. To combat this risk 
of gold-plating, trace requirements back to business objectives to ensure that the new features are 
needed and to select the highest-impact features to implement first. You also might need to prioritize 
enhancement requests against the correction of defects that had been reported against the old 
system.
Also be wary of letting unnecessary new functionality slip into replacement projects. The main 
focus of replacement projects is to migrate existing functionality. However, customers might imagine 
that if you are developing a new system anyway, it is easy to add lots of new capabilities right away. 
Many replacement projects have collapsed because of the weight of uncontrolled scope growth. 
You’re usually better off building a stable first release and adding more features through subsequent 
enhancement projects, provided the first release allows users to do their jobs.
Replacement projects often originate when stakeholders want to add functionality to an existing 
system that is too inflexible to support the growth or has technology limitations. However, there needs 
to be a clear business objective to justify implementing an expensive new system (Devine 2008). Use 
the anticipated cost savings from a new system (such as through reduced maintenance of an old, 
clunky system) plus the value of the new desired functionality to justify a system replacement project.
Also look for existing functionality that doesn’t need to be retained in a replacement system. Don’t 
replicate the existing system’s shortcomings or miss an opportunity to update a system to suit new 
business needs and processes. For example, the BA might ask users, “Do you use <a particular menu 
option>?” If you consistently hear “I never do that,” then maybe it isn’t needed in the replacement 
system. Look for usage data that shows what screens, functions, or data entities are rarely accessed 
in the current system. Even the existing functionality has to map to current and anticipated business 
objectives to warrant re-implementing it in the new system.
Trap Don’t let stakeholders get away with saying “I have it today, so I need it in the new 
system” as a default method of justifying requirements.
Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.
Gap analysis for a replacement project entails understanding existing functionality and discovering 
the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that 
stakeholders want to have re-implemented in the new system. Also, elicit new user requirements that 
the existing system does not address. Consider any change requests that were never implemented CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 397
in the existing system. Prioritize the existing user requirements and the new ones together. Prioritize 
closing the gaps using business objectives as described in the previous section or the other 
prioritization techniques presented in Chapter 16, “First things first: Setting requirement priorities.”
FIGURE 21-1 When you are replacing an existing system, some requirements will be implemented unchanged, 
some will be modified, some will be discarded, and some new requirements might be added.
Maintaining performance levels
Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost 
always have key performance indicators (KPIs) for existing processes that they will want to maintain 
in the new system.

3.5 Glossários (L2)
Em cada iniciativa da ER que envolve mais de uma pessoa, há o risco de falta de um 
entendimento comum da terminologia, ou seja, que algumas pessoas interpretem 
diferentemente os mesmos termos. Para mitigar este problema, o entendimento comum 
dos termos relevantes é registrado em um glossário.
Um glossário é uma coleção central de definições para: termos específicos do contexto, 
termos cotidianos com um significado especial no contexto dado, abreviaturas e acrônimos. 
Os sinônimos (termos diferentes que indicam a mesma coisa) devem ser marcados como 
tal. Os homônimos (usando o mesmo termo para coisas diferentes) devem ser evitados ou 
marcados como tal.
As seguintes regras aplicam-se aos glossários:
▪ Gerenciar o glossário de forma centralizada.
▪ Manter o glossário ao longo de todo o desenvolvimento do sistema.
▪ Definir uma pessoa ou um pequeno grupo responsável pelo glossário.
▪ Usar um estilo e uma estrutura uniformes para o glossário.
▪ Envolver os stakeholders buscando um acordo sobre a terminologia.
▪ Tornar o glossário acessível a todos os envolvidos.
▪ Tornar obrigatório o uso do glossário.
▪ Verificar se os produtos de trabalho respeitam o glossário.

É Stakeholder ou Ator?
Stakeholder = quem tem interesse no sistema (pode não usá-lo diretamente).
Ator (Caso de Uso) = quem INTERAGE diretamente com o sistema.
Todo Ator é Stakeholder; nem todo Stakeholder é Ator.
É Premissa ou Restrição?
Premissa = fato ASSUMIDO como verdadeiro sem confirmação formal. Pode mudar.
Restrição = limite IMPOSTO que não pode ser negociado (lei, orçamento, prazo, tech).
É escopo IN ou OUT?
IN = funcionalidade que o SISTEMA DO PROJETO vai implementar.
OUT = funcionalidade que fica em outro sistema ou versão futura.
Regra prática: se está em outro sistema já existente → OUT.PARTE 4 — Armadilhas Comuns na Extração Automática
Requisito fantasma (Gold Plating)
O documento menciona uma funcionalidade que ninguém pediu explicitamente — foi adicionada 
por quem escreveu o documento como 'boa ideia'. Sinal: funcionalidade descrita sem stakeholder 
associado e sem ligação a um objetivo de negócio.
AÇÃO: extrair como HU/RF com prioridade 'Could have' e sinalizar para validação.
Dois requisitos em uma frase ('e')
'O sistema deve cadastrar e consultar clientes.' → dois RFs distintos.
'O sistema deve ser rápido e seguro.' → dois RNFs distintos.
AÇÃO: sempre separar em IDs distintos quando há 'e' ligando funcionalidades.
Requisito negativo mal formulado
'O sistema não deve perder dados.' → Impreciso. O que é 'perder dados'?
REFORMULAR como: 'O sistema deve persistir todos os dados de pedido mesmo em caso de falha 
de conexão, retomando a gravação quando a conexão for restabelecida.'
AÇÃO: transformar negação em afirmação positiva e verificável.
Cópia literal de linguagem informal
ERRADO: RF-010: 'O sistema tem que ser tipo um CRM mas mais simples.'
A linguagem do documento de entrada nunca deve ir direto para o SRS.
AÇÃO: reformular sempre no padrão 'O sistema deve [verbo] [complemento].'
RNF sem categoria ou sem métrica
Extrair 'o sistema deve ser seguro' e deixar assim é inválido pela ISO 29148.
AÇÃO: identificar a categoria ISO 25010 e propor métrica mínima, marcando [TBD] se o dado 
preciso não estiver no documento.
Confundir processo atual com requisito do novo sistema
Texto descreve como o processo É HOJE, não como deveria ser.
'Hoje o vendedor imprime o pedido e manda por fax' → isso é o estado atual.
O requisito é derivado da MELHORIA desejada, não da cópia do processo ruim.
AÇÃO: identificar a dor/ineficiência → transformar em HU do novo sistema.Stakeholder implícito ignorado
Texto menciona 'o sistema enviará relatório para a contabilidade' — mas 'contabilidade' não foi 
listada como stakeholder. É um usuário secundário implícito.
AÇÃO: varrer o documento inteiro por menções a papéis, departamentos e sistemas externos — 
todos são stakeholders potenciais.

- The system must substantially comply with FFMIA (Federal Financial Management Improvement Act) requirements.
- The general ledger is the central component; every other function depends on it.
- The system must classify and track transactions by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center.
- The system must prevent obligating or spending more than what was actually appropriated (funds control).
- The system must process payments to vendors/payees and confirm that a payment reached the correct destination.
- The system must record and track money owed to the agency (receivables) and follow up when payments are missed.
- The system must support cost management: measuring what programs cost and what they produce.
- The system must produce formal financial statements and reports for management, oversight bodies, and eventual public release.
- Users include financial systems analysts, accountants, program managers, agency operations staff, and periodic auditors.
- The system must be usable by non-technical finance staff, not only by IT staff.
- The system must handle its workload without performance failure and integrate with other existing systems rather than operating in isolation.
- The system must maintain a real audit trail and security controls over who can access what.
- The system must provide adequate web access, rather than restricting users to a single terminal.
- Optional "nice to have" features not mandated by law or regulation are deprioritized in favor of mandatory requirements in the first round.

3. The system generates the formal statement.
4. The accountant selects the oversight export option.
5. The system creates the export file.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The period is not authorized → the system marks the statement as 'Draft'.
fluxos_excecao: 5a. Export validation fails → the system displays the validation errors and does not produce an approved export.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The auditor is authenticated and has audit access.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The auditor retrieves audit events and associated financial records.
fluxo_principal: 1. The auditor selects an audit period, user, action, or record.
2. The system applies the auditor's access scope.
3. The system retrieves matching audit events.
4. The system displays event details and linked records.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. No matching event exists → the system displays 'No audit events found'.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. The requested data is outside the auditor's scope → the system denies access and records the attempt.

casos_de_uso.nome: Exchange data with existing agency system
casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The designated interface is configured and available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The required financial data is exchanged and the integration outcome is recorded.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The exchange is rejected or retried according to the interface error policy.
fluxo_principal: 1. The analyst initiates or schedules a data exchange.
2. The system validates the data structure.
3. The system transmits or receives the data.
4. The system records the integration outcome.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The receiving system is temporarily unavailable → the system marks the exchange as 'Pending retry'.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. Data validation fails → the system rejects the exchange and identifies the invalid records.

gabarito_artefatos.observacoes: Jargao regulatorio/contabil abstrato — claims mantidas o mais literais possivel ao texto original para reduzir risco de interpretacao subjetiva. Fornecedores/beneficiarios e pagadores de valores devidos NAO sao stakeholders (nao logam no sistema, sao partes externas afetadas pelas transacoes). Conteudo em ingles porque o cenario-fonte e em ingles (mesma convencao dos gabaritos RAGAS existentes).

em_escopo: General ledger as the central component of the system
Classifying and tracking transactions by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center
Funds control (preventing obligation/spending above the appropriated amount)
Processing payments to vendors/payees, with confirmation of destination
Recording and following up on amounts owed to the agency, including chasing missed payments
Cost management (what each program costs and produces)
Producing formal financial statements and reports for management, oversight bodies, and eventual public release
A real audit trail and security controls over who can access what
Web access, not restricted to a single terminal
Integration with other existing agency systems
fora_de_escopo: Optional ('nice to have') features not required by law or regulation — deprioritized in the first round in favor of mandatory requirements
premissas: PA-01: [INFERRED] The agency already has other existing systems that the financial system needs to integrate with.
PA-02: The system needs to be in substantial compliance with FFMIA before any eventual formal audit.
restricoes: REST-01 (Regulatory): The system must be in substantial compliance with FFMIA (Federal Financial Management Improvement Act) requirements.
REST-02 (Prioritization): Optional features not required by law or regulation are left out of the first round of development.
REST-03 (Usability): The system must be operable by non-technical finance staff, not only by IT staff.

stakeholders.descricao: Financial systems analyst — day-to-day user of the system.
Accountant — day-to-day user, responsible for accounting records.
Program manager — consults cost and performance data of programs for budget decisions.
Agency operations staff — needs to pull numbers from the system to run the agency.
Auditor — periodically reviews the system to verify compliance and control.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: The system must never allow obligating or spending more than what was actually appropriated (funds control) — a hard, non-negotiable rule.
The general ledger is the central component of the system; every other function depends on it.
Optional features not required by law or regulation are deprioritized relative to mandatory requirements in the first round.

requisitos_funcionais.descricao: The system must maintain a general ledger as its central component, on which the other functions depend.
The system must classify and track transactions by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center.
The system must prevent an obligation or expenditure from exceeding the amount actually appropriated (funds control).
The system must process payments to vendors/payees.
The system must track and confirm that a payment reached the correct destination.
The system must record amounts owed to the agency (receivables).
The system must support following up on/collecting receivables when payment is not made.
The system must support cost management, measuring what each program costs and what it produces.
The system must produce formal financial statements and reports for agency management.
The system must produce formal financial statements and reports for oversight bodies.
The system must support the eventual public release of financial statements and reports.
The system must maintain a real audit trail of who accessed or changed what.
The system must enforce security controls over who can access what.
The system must provide web access to users, instead of restricting them to a single terminal.
The system must integrate with other systems already existing at the agency, instead of operating in isolation.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a financial systems analyst, I want to classify and track transactions by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center, so that program and budget managers can analyze the data.
As an accountant, I want the system to prevent obligations or spending beyond the appropriated amount, so that the agency stays within its funding limits.
As an accounts-payable owner, I want to process payments to vendors/payees and confirm they reached the correct destination, so that disbursements are accurate and traceable.
As an accounts-receivable owner, I want to record amounts owed to the agency and chase overdue payments, so that outstanding amounts are collected.
As a program manager, I want to see cost management data (what a program costs and produces), so that I can support budget decisions.
As agency management, I want formal financial statements and reports, so that I can report to oversight bodies and, eventually, the public.
As an auditor, I want to review a real audit trail and the system's access security controls, so that I can verify compliance during periodic reviews.
As agency operations staff, I want to access the system over the web from multiple locations, so that I'm not restricted to a single terminal.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Record and classify transaction — a user records a financial transaction in the general ledger, classified by fund, program, organization, project, and cost center.
Process vendor payment — the system processes a payment to a vendor/payee and confirms it reached the correct destination, respecting the funds control limit.
Track receivable — the system records an amount owed to the agency and flags it for follow-up when payment is not made.
Generate financial report — a user generates formal financial statements/reports for management, oversight bodies, or public release.
Audit system access — an auditor reviews the system's audit trail and access controls.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a transaction that would exceed the funds appropriated for its fund/program, when it is submitted, then the system prevents the obligation/expenditure from being recorded.
Given a payment issued to a vendor/payee, when the payment is processed, then the system tracks and confirms that it reached the correct destination.
Given a receivable with an overdue payment, when the due date passes without payment, then the system flags the case for follow-up.
Given a request for a formal financial statement, when it is generated, then the result is suitable for submission to management and to oversight bodies.
Given a user accessing the system, when any action is performed, then the system records it in an audit trail that identifies who did what.
